questions.q: What skill does this lesson actually say it's building, regarding CLI/PowerShell automation?
options: Reading and adapting an existing script — recognizing what a command does and changing a parameter — not authoring automation from scratch
Writing production-grade PowerShell modules from a blank file
Memorizing every flag of every az sql subcommand
Replacing all T-SQL knowledge with CLI knowledge
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that most DBAs read and adapt scripts rather than write automation from scratch, and that's the bar this course sets.

questions.q: What does "az sql db list --server myserver --resource-group myrg" do?
options: Returns every database on that server as JSON — useful for a quick inventory pass
Deletes every database on the server
Changes the service tier of every database on the server
Creates a new empty database on the server
questions.explain: list is a read operation returning an inventory, same role as Get-AzSqlDatabase without -DatabaseName in PowerShell.

questions.q: Which command actually changes a database's configuration, per this lesson's CLI example?
options: az sql db update --service-objective S3
az sql db show
az sql db list
az account show
questions.explain: show and list are read-only; update is the command that moves the database to a new service tier.

questions.q: What syntax pattern does the lesson point out between Azure CLI and the Az.Sql PowerShell module?
options: CLI uses --flag value; PowerShell uses -Parameter Value — same underlying operations, different syntax
CLI and PowerShell use identical syntax with no differences
PowerShell cannot perform any operation that the CLI can perform
The CLI only works on Windows, unlike PowerShell
questions.explain: Recognizing that --flag value maps to -Parameter Value is what lets a DBA read scripts in either tool without being intimidated.

questions.q: Why does this lesson explicitly avoid teaching deep PowerShell scripting (loops, error handling, module authoring)?
options: Because most working DBAs get by without it — reading and adapting existing scripts covers the real, recurring need
Because PowerShell cannot be used with Azure SQL at all
Because deep scripting is covered earlier in the T-SQL Development course
Because the DP-300 exam explicitly forbids PowerShell content
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a deliberate scope decision: reading/adapting is the realistic, recurring DBA skill, not building PowerShell modules from scratch.
